pages.name: A steady current
pages.text: A current is a rate: how fast charge flows. One amp is one coulomb each second, so a steady 3 A moves 3 C every second, and in 4 s it moves 3 × 4 = 12 C. On a graph of current against time, that charge is the rectangle under the flat line, 3 A high and 4 s wide. Its area is amps times seconds, which is coulombs. The [[running total]] above adds it up, second by second.

pages.name: A steady speed
pages.task: A boat holds a steady 5 m/s for 6 s, an example. How far does it go?
pages.why: A steady speed times the time it lasts gives the distance: 5 m/s for 6 s is 5 × 6 = 30 m, the area of the rectangle under the flat graph. The height alone, 5, is a speed: how fast, not how far. Adding 5 + 6 adds metres per second to seconds, which gives nothing you can measure.

pages.name: Thinner bars
pages.text: Now the current rises, `i = 3t²` amps from 0 s to 2 s, an example. No single rectangle fits, so cut the time into bars of equal width, each as tall as the current at its start. Each bar is a current times a time, a charge. Four bars 0.5 s wide stand 0, 0.75, 3 and 6.75 A high and give 5.25 C: short, because each flat top misses a thin sliver under the rising curve. Adding up many thin pieces is what an [[integral]] is. Watch the bars thin, then drag the slider yourself.

pages.name: One bar
pages.task: Each bar stands for a current times a time. The bar from 1 s to 1.5 s is 3 A high. How much charge does it stand for?
pages.why: A bar is a current held for a short time, so its charge is its height times its width: 3 A for 0.5 s is 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 C, the bar’s area. Its height alone, 3 A, is how fast charge flows at that moment, not how much has flowed. Adding 3 + 0.5 mixes amps and seconds.

pages.name: The reverse rule
pages.text: Now the reverse rule from the last lesson: the charge is `q = t³ + c`; call it F. The charge that flows is F at the end b take away F at the start a, F(b) − F(a): here (8 + `c`) − (0 + `c`) = 8 C, the number the bars settle on, whatever `c` is. Each step up the curve is one bar’s charge, so the bars climb nearly the whole rise. This is a [[definite integral]], an integral with two ends.

pages.alt: The reverse rule, F: q equals t cubed plus c coulombs. At 2 s: F equals 8 plus c. At 0 s: F equals 0 plus c. F(2) minus F(0) equals (8 plus c) minus (0 plus c) equals 8 C. c equals 3 here: 11 minus 3 equals 8 C. Written the integral from 0 to 2 of 3t squared dt equals 8 C, a definite integral

pages.name: From 1 s to 2 s
pages.task: The same current, `i = 3t²` amps, with the reverse rule `q = t³ + c`. How much charge flows from 1 s to 2 s, `∫₁² 3t² dt`?
pages.why: Put the end time, then the start time, into the reverse rule and subtract: F(2) − F(1) = 8 − 1 = 7 C. 8 C is the charge from 0 s, which counts the first second too. 12 − 3 = 9 puts the times into the current, `3t²`, instead of its reverse rule, `t³`.
pages.alt: The current i equals 3t squared amps, from 1 s to 2 s. Charge from 1 s to 2 s: 7 C. F equals t cubed: F(2) equals 8, F(1) equals 1. F(2) minus F(1) equals 8 minus 1 equals 7 C

pages.name: Mid-height bars
pages.text: Taking each bar’s height at its middle gets close much sooner. Each top then crosses the curve: on the bar’s left half it pokes above the curve, and on its right half the curve rises above it. The extra and the missed slivers nearly cancel, so 4 bars give 7.875 C. On a straight line the two slivers are the same size, so mid-height bars give the exact total. Your MCA papers call this the [[mid-ordinate rule]].

pages.name: Three mid-height bars
pages.task: Three mid-height bars, each 2 s wide, stand under an example speed, `v = t²` m/s, from 0 s to 6 s. How far do the bars say the sports car goes?
pages.why: Each bar is its mid-height times its width, 2 s, so the bars give 2 × (1 + 9 + 25) = 70 m. The reverse rule gives the exact distance, `t³ ÷ 3` at 6 s take away at 0 s, 216 ÷ 3 = 72 m, so three wide bars already land close. Adding the heights alone forgets the width; the tallest bar for all 6 s counts the car at its later speed the whole way.

pages.name: Below the axis
pages.text: A current can flow back. Take `i = 4 − 2t` amps from 0 s to 3 s: it flows forwards until 2 s, then turns negative, and its graph dips below the axis. A negative current times a time is charge taken away, so those bars hang below the axis, hatched, and count as minus: 4 C forwards, then 1 C back, 3 C in all. Count the 1 C back as plus and you get 5 C, more than ever arrived. The reverse rule does the minus for you: `4t − t²` is 12 − 9 = 3 at 3 s and 0 at 0 s.

pages.name: Back to nothing
pages.task: An example current, `i = 3 − t` amps, flows forwards for 3 s, then back for 3 s. What is the net charge from 0 s to 6 s?
pages.why: The bars above the axis add 4.5 C and the bars below take 4.5 C away, so the net charge is 0 C: as much flowed back as flowed forwards. The reverse rule agrees: `3t − t² ÷ 2` is 18 − 18 = 0 at 6 s, and 0 at 0 s. 9 C counts the charge going back as plus; 4.5 C leaves it out.

pages.name: From 1 s to 4 s
pages.task: An example speed, `v = 2t + 3` m/s. How far does the boat go from 1 s to 4 s?
pages.why: Reverse the speed term by term: `2t + 3` becomes `t² + 3t`. At 4 s that is 16 + 12 = 28, and at 1 s it is 1 + 3 = 4, so the boat goes 28 − 4 = 24 m. 28 m is the distance from 0 s, which counts the first second too. 11 − 5 = 6 puts the times into the speed instead of its reverse rule.
pages.alt: A speed, v equals 2t plus 3 m/s, from 1 s to 4 s. Distance from 1 s to 4 s: 24 m. Reverse rule: t squared plus 3t. At 4 s: 28; at 1 s: 4. 28 minus 4 equals 24 m

pages.name: Net charge, 0 s to 5 s
pages.task: An example current, `i = 2t − 4` amps, flows back until 2 s, then forwards. What is the net charge from 0 s to 5 s?
pages.why: The part below the axis, from 0 s to 2 s, is 4 C back; the part above, from 2 s to 5 s, is 9 C forwards; net, 9 − 4 = 5 C. The reverse rule does it at once: `t² − 4t` is 25 − 20 = 5 at 5 s and 0 at 0 s. 13 C counts the charge going back as plus. −5 C takes the end from the start, which flips the sign.
